en: Now follows the Yama-smṛti.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Now follows the description of expiation (prāyaścitta). Therefore, this Dharmaśāstra,
which sets forth the expiations for this Dharma, proceeds for all four castes.

Those who have perished by water, fire, or hanging; those who have fallen from the mendicant life or through fasting; and those who have perished by poison, by leaping from a precipice, or by the stroke of a weapon.
All those who have fallen away and are excluded from all the worlds are purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
Those wicked ones who have fallen from both [paths] and have lost their refuge in the non-village (agrāmya),
are purified by giving two cows and likewise a bull.
Having burned one who has killed a cow or a Brahmin, or one who has died by hanging,
and having cut the very rope [of the hanged], one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
If one is afflicted by maggots born in a wound or bitten by flies and horses,
one should perform half of a *kṛcchra* penance and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability.
When a Brahmin's impurity-duct, which is the source of pus and blood,
becomes a wound infested with worms, he is purified by means of the *mauñjī* oblation.
Any Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra born in the natural order who,
having learned [of this], eats [forbidden food] especially, should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One should determine the size of a morsel to be the measure of a hen’s egg;
otherwise, due to the fault of improper eating, one does not attain purification therein.
One should increase [the morsels] by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease them during the dark fortnight;
on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a Brahmin drinks other types of intoxicants or eats beef, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance; thus his sin is destroyed.
For if the performer should pass away once the penance has been commenced,
he becomes purified on that very day, both in this world and in the next.
As long as one individual, being a separate entity, is purified by penance, the others are not touched by it; they too are all censured.
Those who are unfit to be fed with, unfit to receive gifts from, and unfit to study with, as well as those who have not married—
when they have completed their penance according to the rule, they are all purified and become entitled to inherit property.
For one who is less than eleven years old but more than five years old,
his brother, father, or another relative shall perform the penance.
Therefore, even for one who is most ignorant, there is neither offense nor sin;
there is no royal punishment for him, nor is there any need for expiation.
A child under sixteen years of age,
as well as women and the sick, deserve half of the penance prescribed for those who are eighty years old or more.
When the sun has set and Cāṇḍālas or washerwomen have been touched by some people, what then should be the expiation?
Having bathed and drunk with gold, refined gold, water brought during the day, and water from the sky, all of them are considered pure.
Slaves, barbers, cowherds, family friends, and those who share half the harvest—
these among the Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Those ignorant men who eat the food that is fit to be eaten by a Śūdra incur an expiation;
they should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
When the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter,
the father drinks her menstrual blood month after month.
The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother—
these three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses.
That Brahmin who, deluded by pride, marries such a girl is indeed unfit for conversation and excluded from the ritual row; he is a Brahmin whose wife is a *vṛṣalī*.
A barren woman is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; one whose offspring have died is a *vṛṣalī*;
a Śūdra woman is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; and a maiden who has reached puberty is also a *vṛṣalī*.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by constantly subsisting on alms and reciting prayers for three years.
"She who, having abandoned her own bull (husband), resorts to another man's bull—Bṛhaspati says—that she is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; a Śūdra woman does not become a *vṛṣalī*."
For one who has drunk the saliva of a *vṛṣalī*, for one who has been afflicted by her breath,
and for one who has procreated with her, no atonement whatsoever exists.
Likewise, one who has leucoderma or leprosy, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, a slanderer, and one who is envious; YS 78v.29.

For likewise [unworthy are] the unfortunate, the eunuch, the heretic, the reviler of the Vedas, the sophist, the one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras, and the one who officiates at sacrifices for those for whom it is forbidden.

One who is constantly greedy for receiving gifts, a beggar, one whose nature is attached to sense-objects, one with black teeth, a physician, and likewise one who engages in improper speech; YS78v_31.
These should be avoided with great effort at both funeral rites and acts of giving.
Furthermore, a temple-priest, a hired servant, and a seller of the Vedas—these must be avoided with great effort; so Bhāsvatī has declared.
But he who employs these [unqualified persons] in rites for the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya),
his ancestors depart disappointed, along with the gods and the great seers.
Having seen first the husband of a *māhiṣikā*, then in the middle the husband of a *vṛṣalī*,
and finally the usurer, the ancestors departed in despair.
A wife who is unfaithful is called a *mahiṣī*;
he who tolerates those faults is indeed known as a *māhiṣika*.
He who, having purchased at a fair price, sells at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
As long as the food remains warm, as long as they eat with speech restrained,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned, so long do the ancestors partake of it.
The qualities of the sacrificial offering need not be mentioned when the ancestors have been satiated;
rather, after the ancestors have been satiated, one should subsequently say that the offering was excellent.
As many morsels as one who knows the mantras consumes from the offerings to the gods and ancestors,
so many lumps does his father consume within the body of Brahmā.
A twice-born man who has been touched by one who is impure from eating remnants, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra,
becomes pure by fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one is touched by someone who is not impure from food remnants, only bathing is prescribed;
however, if one is touched by that very person while they are impure from food remnants, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance.
As long as the Brahmins are not honored with food and gold,
so long that sin does not perish, even for one who has observed his vows.
If the body should become wrapped by crows, cranes, or cilla-birds, or smeared with impurities,
and [these] should enter the limbs or the mouth, purification for one struck by such contamination occurs through a thorough bath.
If any part of the body above the navel— excluding the two hands—
is defiled, it becomes pure by that much alone through bathing above and cleansing below.
If one consumes things that are not to be eaten, drunk, or licked,
as well as semen, urine, or feces, what shall be the expiation?
Having drunk the water of the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, the kuśa grass, the aśvattha, and the palāśa— by doing so, one becomes pure in just six nights.

A Brahmin who has fallen away from the life of a wandering mendicant, having maintained the sacred fires during times of non-distress, may wish to return to the state of a householder while remaining one who has not formally re-established the sacrificial fires.
One should perform three *kṛcchra* penances and also observe *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts;
such a person deserves to undergo the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) again, beginning with the *jātakarman* as prescribed.
Having dried out mattresses, pillows, flowers, and red garments by means of heat, one becomes pure after sprinkling them with water.
Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the occasion, and the state, one should practice the Dharma.
Roads, mud, water, boats, iron, grass,
and structures built of baked bricks are purified by wind and the sun.
When a sick person has reached the point of needing a bath, one who is not sick should bathe ten times;
by bathing again and again and touching that person, the sick person will then become pure.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
as well as the fisherman, the Meda, and the Bhilla— these seven are remembered as the lowest-born (antyaja).
Having gone to these women, one should indeed perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
When there occurs contact between women who are menstruating, whether it be mutual touching or not,
how is the expiation prescribed for them according to each respective caste?
Having touched a woman in her menses, or one of the same lineage, or one who has a husband,
whether intentionally or unintentionally, one becomes pure by bathing and waiting for the prescribed time.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman and a Śūdra-born woman touch each other while in their menses,
the former is purified by the Kṛcchra penance, while the Śūdra woman is purified by a quarter-penance.
If a Kṣatriya woman and a Śūdra woman who have both reached their menses touch one another,
the former shall perform a penance lacking one quarter, while the latter shall likewise perform a penance lacking half a quarter.
If a woman born of a Vaiśya and one born of a Śūdra touch each other while in their menses,
the former shall perform a quarter *kṛcchra* penance, and the latter half of that.
If she is touched by a dog, a jackal, a monkey, or a donkey while in her menses, she shall remain without food for that long; having bathed at the proper time, she becomes pure.
If a woman who is not menstruating is touched by some *caṇḍālas* while she is in her menses,
she becomes pure through the *prājāpatya* penance, the *kṛcchra* penance, and one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
If a Brahmin has been touched at night by a woman in her courses, by an outcaste,
or by water brought during the day, he should bathe in the presence of the sacred fire.
Water touched by the rays of the sun during the day, by the rays of the stars at night,
and by the twilight of both morning and evening, is always pure.
If a twice-born man drinks water touched by his fingernails during the ritual sipping (ācamana),
he clearly drinks liquor, according to the word of Yama.
Likewise, [the same applies] to a well or a pond, as well as to a well with stones, by striking with weapons,
by striking with a staff, or with a lump of clay and a herd of cows.
In confinement and in bondage, likewise when placed upon a large wooden tree, in a narrow passage, and with ropes or garments; (Yogācārabhūmi 78v.67).
All this has been told to you regarding the supreme occasions of negligence;
wherever cows have died, one should perform the appropriate expiation.
In the case of a violent killing, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; with stones, it shall be double.
In the case of a pit, it is half a *kṛcchra*, but for a tree, it is a quarter *kṛcchra*.
For a blow with a weapon, one should perform three *kṛcchra* penances; for a blow with a staff, one should perform two.
Even if he strikes a cow with a cloth only with great difficulty,
he who dwells among cows near a river or a wilderness is purified.
On the first day one should shave the body hair; on the second, the beard;
on the third, the top-knot should be maintained; and on the fourth, one should shave including the top-knot.
One should not perform the shaving of women's heads, nor should she follow a cow [into the forest].
She should not stay overnight in a cow-pen, nor should she recite Vedic scripture.
Having pulled out all the hair, one should cut off two finger-breadths;
in this very manner, the shaving of the head for women is prescribed.
If one is born dead, there is birth-impurity for both [the father and mother];
however, if one is defiled by a mortal sin, there is no birth-impurity for him.
Indeed, one should avoid four activities during the twilight hours:
eating, sexual intercourse, sleep, and fourthly, the private recitation of sacred texts.
From food, disease arises; from sexual intercourse, a cruel womb [is conceived];
sleep turns away from prosperity; and through self-study, death is certain.
Out of ignorance, O best of the twice-born, and with the desire for the welfare of the social orders, this scripture has been proclaimed by me; listen to it with careful attention.
Thus ends the Dharmaśāstra proclaimed by Yama.
